The filters are bare functions and it's getting hard to attach metadata to them. Introduce a proper abstraction: create pipeline/base.py with a Filter base class -- subclasses declare a class attribute `name` (the public registry name) and implement `apply(self, text)` returning the transformed text. Convert every function in pipeline/filters.py into a Filter subclass with exactly the same transformation semantics (the module docstring spells them out -- keep them bit-identical). The registry should now hand out Filter INSTANCES, and Pipeline must work with them. Keep backwards compatibility: the old plain functions (strip_edges, lowercase, uppercase, collapse_spaces) must still be importable from pipeline.filters and still work as plain str-to-str calls -- make them thin wrappers over the new classes. The CLI must keep working, and keep the seed tests green (update them if they construct pipelines the old way).

Maintaining the registry dict by hand keeps causing merge conflicts. Add a `register` decorator to pipeline/registry.py: putting @register on a Filter subclass instantiates it and stores the instance under its `name`, then returns the class. Registering a name that is already taken must raise ValueError. Register all existing filters with the decorator. Keep the old manual FILTERS dict honored for now (people have scripts that stuff entries into it): get_filter(name) checks the decorator registry first, then falls back to FILTERS -- and that fallback should emit a DeprecationWarning. Also add available() returning the sorted list of all usable filter names from both sources, with no duplicates.

We're standardizing verbs across our tools: rename Pipeline.process to Pipeline.run. Keep process() as a deprecation shim that emits a DeprecationWarning and delegates to run() so old callers don't break yet. Move every internal caller inside the package (the CLI, the tests, anything else) over to run() so only external code still hits the shim.

filters.py is getting crowded and we're about to add more. Split it into a pipeline/filters/ subpackage organized by category: pipeline/filters/text.py holds the case transforms (lowercase, uppercase) and pipeline/filters/spacing.py holds the whitespace ones (strip_edges, collapse_spaces). Delete the old flat module. Compatibility matters: `from pipeline.filters import lowercase` (and the other three old names) must keep working via re-exports in the subpackage's __init__, and merely importing pipeline (or pipeline.filters) must still trigger registration of every filter so get_filter works without any extra imports.

Add config-driven defaults. The CLI should accept --config PATH (default: pipeline.json in the current directory) pointing at a JSON file shaped like {"default_chain": ["strip_edges", "collapse_spaces", "lowercase"]}. When --filters is not given, use the config's default_chain; if --filters is absent AND the config file doesn't exist, exit with a nonzero status and a clear error. --filters stops being required. Also add a classmethod Pipeline.from_names(names) that builds a pipeline by looking each name up in the registry (unknown names propagate the registry's KeyError) -- and use it in the CLI. Ship a pipeline.json at the repo root containing exactly that example chain.

New filter category: word-level filters. Add pipeline/filters/tokens.py following the established pattern (Filter subclass, decorator registration, auto-registered when the package is imported) with two filters. dedupe_words (name 'dedupe_words'): split the text on whitespace, drop repeated words keeping only each word's first occurrence, and join with single spaces. sort_words (name 'sort_words'): split on whitespace, sort the words alphabetically (duplicates kept), join with single spaces. Both must show up in available() and be usable from the CLI and from Pipeline.from_names like every other filter.

Two bug reports from the same downstream user. First: back when the manual FILTERS dict was the way in, their startup code registered everything itself, and when they migrated to our decorator they kept an explicit register(...) call on each of our filter classes as a belt-and-braces step. So each of those classes now reaches register twice -- once from the decorator when the package is imported, once from their explicit call -- and the ValueError we added kills their startup with 'already registered'. Make registration idempotent: register applied to the SAME class that already owns the name is a harmless no-op, while a DIFFERENT class claiming an existing name must still raise ValueError, and either way available() must never list a name twice. Second: their CI runs everything under python -W error::DeprecationWarning and they want a guarantee our package is clean there -- importing pipeline, running the CLI (both with --filters and via the config default chain), and Pipeline.from_names must not trigger any DeprecationWarning. The only places a warning may originate are the genuinely deprecated surfaces themselves, i.e. an external caller invoking process() or going through the manual-dict fallback.

Everyone downstream has migrated, so drop the deprecated surface entirely. Remove the process() shim from Pipeline -- only run() remains, and a Pipeline instance must not even have a process attribute anymore. Remove the manual FILTERS dict from pipeline/registry.py along with its fallback in get_filter -- an unknown name now just raises KeyError, with the available filter names included in the message. Remove the legacy flat re-exports and wrapper functions from the filters subpackage: strip_edges, lowercase, uppercase and collapse_spaces must no longer be importable from pipeline.filters -- filters live only in their category modules and the registry now. After the cleanup: importing pipeline (or pipeline.filters) must still auto-register every filter, the CLI with the config default chain and --filters must keep working exactly as before, no DeprecationWarning may fire on import or any normal use, and update tests/test_seed.py so it exercises only the surviving API and still passes. Nothing anywhere in the package may still reference a removed name.
